Chapter 4 · 第四章

Running One-on-Ones with Your Team与团队开展一对一沟通

— PDF p.101 —

One of the very first things I do when stepping into a tech lead role with a new team is set up recurring one-on-ones with each team member. While the collaborative dynamic of the team as a whole is essential, these individual one-on-ones are where you can build personal connections, understand unique perspectives, and address concerns that might not surface in group settings. Before diving into the tech stack, analyzing the codebase, or meeting stakeholders, I prioritize these meetings, because the team's collective success starts with understanding and supporting each individual.

当我以技术负责人的身份加入一个新团队时，最先做的事情之一，就是和每位团队成员安排定期的一对一沟通。虽然团队整体的协作氛围至关重要，但正是在这些一对一的交流中，你才能建立私人联系、了解每个人独特的视角，并处理那些在集体场合里不会浮现出来的顾虑。在钻研技术栈、分析代码库或会见干系人之前，我会优先安排这些会面，因为团队的集体成功，始于理解和支持每一个人。

That said, there's an important distinction worth calling out early. In some companies, one-on-ones are formally owned by engineering managers, and that can lead to some confusion about whether tech leads should still run their own. My view is simple: yes, you absolutely should. Even if there's some overlap in topics, that doesn't mean the conversations are redundant. It just means you'll need strong alignment with your EM and clarity with your team about your role in supporting them.

话虽如此，有一个重要区别值得尽早点明。在有些公司，一对一是由工程经理（EM）正式负责的，这会让人困惑：技术负责人是否还需要自己再做一对一？我的看法很简单：当然需要。即便话题上有重叠，也不意味着这些对话是多余的。它只意味着你需要和 EM 保持高度一致，并让团队清楚你在支持他们这件事上所扮演的角色。

Take growth, for example. An EM might manage the formal side, including things like promotions, compensation processes, and official career frameworks, but that doesn't mean people's growth isn't also your responsibility. Quite the opposite. Their development impacts the team's outcomes, and by extension, your success as a lead. As someone who works closely with them day to day, you're often in a better position than the EM to support their progress in practical, immediate ways. That's why these conversations matter, regardless of reporting lines.

以成长为例。EM 可能负责正式的那一面，包括晋升、薪酬流程和官方的职业框架，但这并不意味着员工的成长就不是你的责任。恰恰相反。他们的成长直接影响团队的产出，进而影响你作为负责人的成败。作为每天和他们紧密共事的人，你往往比 EM 更有条件以实际、即时的方式支持他们进步。这就是为什么无论汇报线如何划分，这些对话都很重要。

These early conversations set the tone for your working relationships and help you establish trust and rapport from day one.

这些早期的对话为你们的工作关系定下基调，帮你从第一天起就建立信任与融洽的关系。

— PDF p.102 —

In this chapter, I'll walk you through how to get the most out of one-on-ones: how to structure them, what to talk about, how to build trust, and how to avoid common pitfalls. Whether you're new to the role or looking to uplevel how you approach these conversations, the ideas in this chapter are designed to help you make every one-on-one count, for both you and your team.

在本章中，我会带你了解如何把一对一沟通的价值发挥到最大：如何组织、聊些什么、如何建立信任，以及如何避开常见的坑。无论你是刚上任，还是想提升自己开展这些对话的方式，本章的思路都旨在帮你让每一次一对一都真正有价值——无论是对你还是对团队。

The Value of One-on-Ones一对一沟通的价值

One-on-ones are the most powerful tool you have as a tech lead. They will make your life easier, strengthen your relationships, and support the growth of your team members.

一对一是你作为技术负责人所能拥有的最强大的工具。它们会让你的工作更轻松、巩固你的人际关系，并支持团队成员的成长。

First, they help you stay ahead of potential issues. One-on-ones create space to deliver feedback, identify underlying problems, and even find tasks to delegate. They give you a better understanding of what's really going on in your team and help you tackle challenges before they escalate.

首先，它们帮你提前发现潜在问题。一对一为你创造了反馈、识别深层问题、甚至找到可以授权出去的任务的空间。它们让你更清楚团队里真实发生着什么，帮你在挑战升级之前就着手处理。

Second, they strengthen relationships. These conversations allow you to connect with your team members individually, creating a space for trust and open dialogue. The questions they ask and the feedback they share offer invaluable insights into their interests, concerns, and goals.

其次，它们强化关系。这些对话让你能和每位团队成员单独建立联结，为信任和坦诚交流创造空间。他们提出的问题、分享的反馈，会让你极其宝贵地洞察到他们的兴趣、顾虑和目标。

Finally, they drive growth. One-on-ones are where you provide the guidance and support your team members need to take on new challenges and develop their skills. They're a direct investment in the team's success, and yours.

最后，它们推动成长。正是在一对一里，你提供团队成员迎接新挑战、发展技能所需的指导与支持。这是对团队成功的直接投资，也是对你自己成功的直接投资。

MAKE YOUR LIFE EASIER让你的工作更轻松

One-on-ones aren't just for your team members; they're for you, too.

一对一不只是为团队成员准备的，也是为你自己准备的。

Ever had feedback you wanted to give but kept putting off? A one-on-one is the perfect space to deliver it. It's your chance to stop waiting and address things before they grow into bigger problems (although timely feedback should never be replaced; more on this in the section "How to Give Useful Feedback to Your Team" on page 116).

你有没有过一直想给、却一拖再拖的反馈？一对一就是送出它的完美场合。这是你停止等待、在问题变大之前就把它处理掉的机会（不过，及时的反馈永远不应被一对一取代；更多内容见第 116 页"如何向团队提供有用的反馈"一节）。

They're also a window into what's happening behind the scenes. You'll pick up on things that don't surface in team meetings: frustrations, potential conflicts, or underlying issues. For example, during a one-on-one, a team member might express frustration over unclear expectations from another department, something they wouldn't feel comfortable raising in a group setting. This gives you the chance to address the issue privately, clarify responsibilities, and prevent a broader misunderstanding from escalating. Asking the right questions helps you uncover and resolve these issues early.

它们也是一扇窗，让你看到幕后正在发生什么。你会察觉到团队会议上不会浮现的东西：沮丧、潜在冲突或深层问题。例如，在一对一里，某位团队成员可能会表达对另一个部门期望不清的不满——这种事他们在集体场合里不好意思提出来。这就让你有机会私下处理问题、厘清职责，防止更广泛的误解升级。提出恰当的问题，能帮你及早发现并解决这些问题。

— PDF p.103 —

And let's not forget delegation. Want to get some things off your plate? Use one-on-ones to share what you're working on and see what sparks interest. Ask, "Would you be interested in taking over this initiative?" You'll be surprised how often someone is eager to step up.

还有授权这件事也别忘。想把一些事从自己肩上卸下来？利用一对一分享你正在做的事，看看哪些能点燃别人的兴趣。问一句："你有没有兴趣接手这个项目？"你会惊讶地发现，很多时候都有人渴望站出来承担。

One-on-ones also give you a unique view into your team. Pay attention to the questions your team members ask; they're often just as revealing as their answers. For example:

一对一还让你对团队拥有独特的视角。留意团队成员提出的问题；这些问题往往和他们的回答一样能说明问题。例如：

  • "How am I doing in this area?" signals they're keen to grow and want your guidance."我在这个领域做得怎么样？"——这表明他们渴望成长，希望得到你的指导。
  • "What's happening with [initiative]?" might mean they're looking for ways to contribute more or feel left out of the loop."[某个项目]进展如何？"——可能意味着他们想寻找更多贡献的机会，或者感觉自己被排除在信息圈之外。

These moments open doors to conversations that help you understand your team better, identify their motivations, and anticipate potential challenges.

这些瞬间会打开对话之门，帮你更好地理解团队、识别他们的动力来源，并预判潜在的挑战。

One-on-ones are like your leadership cheat code. When you invest time in understanding your team and building strong relationships, you'll find it easier to align on goals, address conflicts, and keep everyone moving forward together.

一对一就像是你的领导力作弊码。当你投入时间去理解团队、建立牢固关系时，你会发现更容易在目标上达成一致、化解冲突，并让大家一起向前。

STRENGTHEN INDIVIDUAL RELATIONSHIPS强化个人关系

In Chapter 3, I talked about how important it is to build strong connections with your team and the impact those relationships have on your team's results. One-on-ones are one of the best tools you have to build those relationships.

在第 3 章里，我谈到了与团队建立牢固联系有多么重要，以及这些关系对团队成果的影响。一对一正是你用来建立这些关系的最佳工具之一。

These conversations go beyond surface-level work interactions. They create a dedicated space for trust and open dialogue. Showing up consistently for one-on-ones sends a clear message: "I value your time, your input, and you as a person." It's not just about work updates; it's about showing you care, whether it's chatting about their weekend plans or diving into their career goals.

这些对话超越了表面的工作互动。它们为信任和坦诚交流创造了一个专门的空间。始终如一地出现在一对一里，会传递一个清晰的信号："我重视你的时间、你的意见，也重视你这个人。"这不只是工作进展汇报；更是在表达你在乎——无论是聊聊他们周末的计划，还是深入探讨他们的职业目标。

One-on-ones also give you the chance to connect with your team members individually, in a way group settings never can. Talking about personal interests, challenges, or aspirations helps to humanize the relationship and build a stronger bond over time.

一对一还让你有机会以集体场合永远无法做到的方式，与每位团队成员单独建立联结。聊聊个人兴趣、挑战或抱负，能让关系变得更有人情味，并随着时间建立更牢固的纽带。

And that's why canceling one-on-ones is one of the fastest ways to break trust. If you make a habit of pushing them aside, it sends the message that other things are more important than your team members. Of course, emergencies happen, but canceling without a solid reason, or doing it repeatedly, is a clear recipe to erode the connection you've worked to build.

这也是为什么取消一对一是摧毁信任最快的方式之一。如果你习惯性地把它们推到一边，传递出的信号就是：别的事情都比你的团队成员更重要。当然，紧急情况在所难免，但没有充分理由就取消、或者反复取消，显然会一点点侵蚀你苦心建立起来的联结。

— PDF p.104 —

Commit to these meetings and prioritize them. They are your chance to strengthen relationships, understand your team on a deeper level, and build the foundation for collaboration and trust.

请承诺投入这些会议，并把它们排在优先位置。这是你强化关系、更深地理解团队、为协作与信任打下基础的机会。

SUPPORT PEOPLE'S GROWTH支持员工成长

The tech lead role varies widely across organizations; sometimes it includes formal line management and other times it's a senior IC position without direct people management responsibilities. Regardless of where your role falls on that spectrum, one thing remains true: supporting the growth of your team members is part of the job. Their development directly influences the team's outcomes, and, by extension, your success as a lead.

技术负责人这个角色在不同组织里差异很大：有时它包含正式的直线管理，有时则是一个没有直接管人职责的高级 IC（个人贡献者）岗位。无论你的角色落在这个光谱的哪一端，有一点始终不变：支持团队成员的成长是你工作的一部分。他们的发展直接影响团队的产出，进而影响你作为负责人的成败。

One-on-ones are a golden opportunity to support that growth.

一对一是支持这种成长的绝佳机会。

Start by emphasizing the value of a growth plan (see the section "Developing a Personal Growth Plan" on page 38). If your team members don't have one, help them define it. Talk about the skills they want to develop, areas they want to improve, and how their growth aligns with the team's goals.

可以先强调成长计划的价值（见第 38 页"制定个人成长计划"一节）。如果团队成员还没有，就帮他们一起定一个。聊聊他们想发展哪些技能、想改进哪些方面，以及他们的成长如何与团队目标对齐。

Once you have a clear sense of what growth looks like for each individual, mentoring and coaching become two of the most effective ways to help them get there. Before diving deeper, it's worth addressing a common question: what's the difference between mentoring and coaching, and which one should I be doing as a tech lead? See Table 4-1 for a breakdown.

一旦你清楚了对每个人而言成长是什么样子，导师制（mentoring）和教练制（coaching）就成了帮他们到达目标最有效的两种方式。在深入之前，值得先回答一个常见问题：导师和教练有什么区别？作为技术负责人我该做哪一个？对照表 4-1。

Table 4-1. Difference between a mentor and a coach

表 4-1. 导师与教练的区别

Mentor / 导师Coach / 教练
Shares experiences, opens doors, offers guidance and advice.分享经验、敞开大门、提供指导和建议。Helps others discover solutions, supports journeys, challenges their thinking.帮助他人自己发现解决方案、支持成长历程、挑战他们的思维方式。
Better suited for junior developers: "When I faced a similar issue, I found that breaking it down like this helped. Would you like me to walk you through it?"更适合初级开发者："我遇到类似问题时，发现这样拆解很有帮助。要不要我带你过一遍？"Better suited for senior developers who have experience but need help choosing the right approach: "What options have you considered? What do you think might work best and why?"更适合有经验、但需要帮助选择正确方法的高级开发者："你考虑过哪些选项？你觉得哪种可能最有效？为什么？"

At their core, mentors and coaches are tools to support growth, but they differ in approach. Mentoring often involves giving advice. People come to you for your expertise and experience; they expect your input. That's perfectly valid. Just remember: your experience might not map directly to theirs, so after you share, help them reflect on how it applies to their situation and what they might take from it.

从本质上说，导师和教练都是支持成长的工具，但方式不同。导师制往往意味着给出建议。人们来找你，是冲着你的专长和经验；他们期待你的看法。这完全没问题。只需记住：你的经验未必能直接套用到他们身上，所以分享之后，要帮他们思考这些经验如何应用于他们的处境、他们可以从中借鉴什么。

— PDF p.105 —

Coaching, on the other hand, treats advice as a last resort. Instead of offering answers, it leans on asking deeper questions to help the other person uncover their own solutions. In fact, when I find myself in a coaching conversation, I often say, "Let's explore this together, and if by the end you still feel stuck, I'll share my take." Most of the time, they find their own answer; they just need someone to help them navigate toward it.

而教练制则把建议当作最后手段。它不直接给答案，而是靠提出更深入的问题，帮对方自己发现解决方案。事实上，当我进入一次教练式对话时，我常说："我们一起来探索这个问题，如果聊到最后你仍然觉得卡住了，我再分享我的看法。"大多数时候，他们会找到自己的答案；他们只是需要有人帮自己一步步走过去。

Tip: For a practical introduction to coaching, The Coaching Habit by Michael Bungay Stanier (Page Two) offers a simple framework of powerful questions that any leader can start using right away; no formal coaching background is required.

提示：想入门教练法，可以读 Michael Bungay Stanier 的《The Coaching Habit》（Page Two 出版）。它提供了一套简单有力的提问框架，任何管理者都可以立刻上手使用，不需要任何正式的教练背景。

That said, don't get too hung up on definitions. As a tech lead, you don't need to obsess over whether you're being a coach or a mentor in a given moment. What matters is utilizing the techniques each of them brings to the table to support your team's growth.

话虽如此，也不要太纠结于定义。作为技术负责人，你不必在某一刻反复琢磨自己到底是在当教练还是当导师。重要的是运用二者各自的技巧来支持团队成长。

Both methods are focused on helping others grow, and one of the first things they offer is accountability.

两种方式都聚焦于帮助他人成长，而它们带来的第一件事，就是"问责与跟进"（accountability）。

To provide accountability, start by helping your team members articulate clear, realistic goals. Then, make a habit of following up on them regularly in your one-on-ones. A simple check-in like "Last time you said you wanted to get more confident in system design interviews. How's that going?" shows you're paying attention and that their growth matters.

要做到跟进问责，先帮团队成员把清晰、现实的目标讲清楚。然后养成习惯，在一对一里定期跟进这些目标。一句简单的跟进——比如"上次你说想在系统设计面试上更有把握，现在进展怎么样？"——就表明你在留心，他们的成长对你很重要。

You can also build light structures to keep them on track: note goals and progress in your shared one-on-one doc, set gentle reminders, or suggest small milestones. Even offering to review something they're working on or scheduling a future follow-up creates a sense of rhythm.

你也可以搭一些轻量的结构来帮他们保持在轨道上：在共享的一对一文档里记下目标和进展、设置温和的提醒、或者建议一些小的里程碑。哪怕只是主动提出帮他们看看正在做的东西、或者约定以后再跟进一次，都能营造出一种节奏感。

Both mentoring and coaching rely heavily on active listening: being fully present, asking thoughtful questions, and understanding what your team member truly needs. (See the section "Create a Safe Space" on page 97 for specific strategies on building active listening habits.)

导师制和教练制都高度依赖积极倾听（active listening）：全情投入、提出有思考的问题、理解团队成员真正需要什么。（关于培养积极倾听习惯的具体策略，见第 97 页"营造安全空间"一节。）

Once you've created this space for reflection and exploration, one-on-ones become a great setting to uncover opportunities for delegation, which is a key way to support growth in practice. Pay attention to where someone is eager to stretch, or simply ask, "What kind of projects would you like to take more ownership of?" Then look for opportunities that align with their interests and goals. For instance: "I've been working on this initiative, but I think it could be a great opportunity for you. Would you be interested in leading it?"

一旦你创造了这种供反思和探索的空间，一对一就成了发现授权机会的绝佳场合——而授权正是在实践中支持成长的关键方式。留意哪里有人渴望进一步挑战自己，或者直接问："你想更多地负责哪类项目？"然后寻找与他们兴趣和目标相匹配的机会。例如："我一直在推进这个项目，但我觉得对你来说可能是个很好的机会。你有没有兴趣牵头做？"

— PDF p.106 —

One-on-ones also create a natural, lower-pressure environment for sharing feedback, both positive and improving points. You might say, "I really appreciated how you handled that conversation with the client, especially how you clarified expectations early on. It set a great tone." Or, when addressing something more difficult: "You mentioned wanting to get better at leading technical discussions. I noticed you stayed a bit quiet during yesterday's architecture review. How are you feeling about jumping in during those conversations?"

一对一还为分享反馈创造了一个自然、低压力的环境——无论正面反馈还是改进意见。你可以说："我很欣赏你处理和客户那次对话的方式，尤其是你一开始就把期望讲清楚了，开了个很好的头。"或者在谈更难的话题时："你之前提到想更擅长主持技术讨论。我注意到昨天架构评审时你话不多。你对在这类讨论里更主动地参与，感觉怎么样？"

Making growth a priority in your one-on-ones is an investment in your team. Whether through mentoring, coaching, finding delegation opportunities, or providing feedback, your team members will feel supported and empowered to take on new challenges, which will speed up their growth.

把成长作为一对一的优先事项，是对团队的投资。无论是通过导师指导、教练式引导、寻找授权机会，还是提供反馈，团队成员都会感到被支持、被赋能，从而敢于迎接新挑战，这会加速他们的成长。

Set Up Your One-on-Ones for Success让一对一沟通从一开始就步入正轨

Before jumping into the strategies for setting up impactful one-on-ones, it's important to take a step back and clarify your role and make sure your team understands it too. In some teams, the tech lead also acts as the line manager. In others, there's a separate engineering manager or team lead who formally handles things like performance reviews and career progression. The split varies widely across organizations, and that's OK, as long as expectations are clear.

在跳入"如何安排有成效的一对一"的具体策略之前，有必要先退一步，厘清你自己的角色，并确保团队也理解这个角色。在有些团队里，技术负责人同时也是直线经理；在另一些团队里，则另有一位工程经理或团队负责人，正式负责绩效评估和职业发展这类事。这种划分在不同组织里差异很大，这都没关系，只要期望清晰就行。

Even if you don't own formal responsibilities like compensation or promotions, you still play a huge role in your team members' growth. In fact, I'd argue that supporting that growth is part of your job. Your involvement might look different depending on the setup. For example, your conversations might not directly feed into performance reviews. Nevertheless, the mindset still applies: you are a key part of how your team develops. Chapter 7 goes deeper into how to contribute to reviews even if you're not the direct manager.

即便你不负责薪酬、晋升这类正式职责，你在团队成员的成长中仍然扮演着重要角色。事实上，我认为支持这种成长本身就是你工作的一部分。根据组织架构的不同，你参与的方式可能不一样。例如，你的对话可能不会直接进入绩效评估。但即便如此，这个心态依然成立：你是团队成长方式中关键的一环。第 7 章会更深入地讨论：即便你不是直属经理，如何为评估贡献力量。

— PDF p.107 —

That's why the kinds of conversations described in this chapter are valuable in both contexts. Whether you're mentoring a junior developer, coaching someone through a tough technical challenge, or helping clarify next steps in someone's growth, you have influence. These one-on-ones are where much of that impact happens.

这就是为什么本章所描述的这类对话在两种情形下都有价值。无论你是在指导初级开发者、在陪某个人攻克一个棘手的技术难题，还是在帮人理清成长的下一步，你都拥有影响力。而这种影响力，很大一部分正是在这些一对一中发生的。

Now, let's look at how to set those one-on-ones up for success.

现在，我们来看看如何让这些一对一从一开始就走向成功。

Making the most of your one-on-ones doesn't require overly complicated strategies. In fact, the biggest impact often comes from sticking to a few straightforward principles. But as simple as these may seem, many tech leads struggle to apply them consistently.

把一对一做好，并不需要多么复杂的策略。事实上，最大的效果往往来自坚持几条简单直接的原则。但尽管这些原则看起来简单，许多技术负责人却难以始终如一地践行。

The foundation of successful one-on-ones starts with consistency. Whether weekly, biweekly, or monthly, they need a regular cadence. Sporadic check-ins won't cut it. Clear expectations are equally important; both you and your team members should understand what to expect from these conversations. Focused discussions help keep the meetings valuable by addressing the right topics. Trust and collaboration are built when the space feels safe for team members to share openly. Last, follow-through is critical: track action items and revisit previous discussions to ensure progress and accountability.

成功一对一的基石是"一致性"。无论每周、每双周还是每月，都需要固定的节奏。断断续续的碰面谈不到点子上。清晰的期望同样重要；你和团队成员都应该清楚这些对话能带来什么。聚焦的讨论通过谈对话题，让会议保持价值。当空间让团队成员感到安全、可以坦诚分享时，信任与协作才得以建立。最后，跟进落地至关重要：跟踪待办事项、回顾之前的讨论，确保进展与问责。

In the next sections, I'll break down each of these principles and share practical ways to implement them, so you can make your one-on-ones as impactful as possible.

接下来的几节，我会逐一拆解这些原则，并分享落地的实用方法，帮你把一对一的效果发挥到最大。

STICK TO A REGULAR CADENCE坚持固定的节奏

The single most important factor for successful one-on-ones is consistency. Yet, it's one of the areas where tech leads often fall short.

成功一对一最重要的单一因素，就是一致性。然而，这恰恰是技术负责人最常做得不到位的地方之一。

Regular, predictable one-on-ones create a foundation of trust. Whether you meet weekly, biweekly, or monthly, the cadence needs to be reliable.

规律、可预期的一对一，会打下信任的基础。无论每周、每双周还是每月见一次，这个节奏都必须可靠。

I recommend meeting with each team member every two weeks for 30 minutes. For a team of up to eight people, this means scheduling four one-on-ones one week and four the next, which works out to just two hours per week, a manageable commitment.

我建议每两周和每位团队成员谈一次，每次 30 分钟。对于一个最多八个人的团队，这意味着一周安排四次一对一、下周再安排四次，算下来每周只占用两小时，是可以承受的投入。

Of course, the size of your team will influence what's realistic. My ideal team size for one tech lead is a maximum of eight people. This number makes it possible to keep up the biweekly schedule while staying deeply connected to the team.

当然，团队大小会影响什么才现实。我认为一位技术负责人理想的团队规模最多是八个人。这个数字让人既能维持双周一次的节奏，又能和团队保持紧密的联系。

For larger teams, maintaining this cadence can be more challenging. In those cases, it becomes even more important to be intentional about how you adapt your one-on-one schedule to make sure everyone still feels supported and seen. Here are some strategies that tech leads use in these situations:

对于更大的团队，维持这个节奏会更有挑战。这种情况下，你更需要有意识地调整一对一的安排，确保每个人仍然感到被支持、被看见。以下是技术负责人在这种情况下常用的一些策略：

Reduce frequency降低频率

Shift to a three-week rotation instead of two. Spread out the one-on-ones to avoid burnout while still maintaining regular touchpoints.

改成三周一次的节奏，而不是两周。把一对一错开安排，避免自己疲于奔命，同时仍然保持定期接触。

You can also ask people directly what cadence and duration works best for them. The problem might solve itself through conversation; some people you think need more contact may actually prefer less, and vice versa.

你也可以直接问大家，什么样的频率和时长对他们最合适。问题可能在对话中就自行化解了：有些你以为需要更多接触的人，其实更喜欢少一些，反之亦然。

— PDF p.108 —

That said, reducing frequency can impact the strength of the relationship, so it should be a carefully considered trade-off. Just make sure to set the right expectations and align with your team before making any changes: explain the reasoning behind it and ensure everyone is on the same page.

话虽如此，降低频率会影响关系的紧密程度，所以这应当是一个经过深思熟虑的权衡。在做出任何改变之前，务必设定正确的预期、和团队对齐：解释背后的原因，确保大家都理解一致。

Shorten the duration缩短时长

Many tech leads default to 60-minute meetings, but half an hour is often enough when you stay focused. A shorter, consistent one-on-one is far more effective than an hour-long meeting that frequently gets postponed or canceled.

许多技术负责人默认开 60 分钟，但只要保持专注，半小时往往就够了。一次更短、但稳定坚持的一对一，远比一场动辄被推迟或取消的一小时会议有效。

I generally advise against going below 30 minutes. Anything less tends to feel rushed and doesn't give enough space for meaningful conversation or deeper check-ins.

我一般不建议低于 30 分钟。再短就容易让人感到仓促，也没有足够空间进行有意义的对话或更深入的关切。

Adapt frequency by need根据需要调整频率

Prioritize newer team members or those who need more support. For example, schedule more frequent one-on-ones for new joiners and reduce them for senior members who are already well-established (as long as they agree with this).

把优先级给新成员或需要更多支持的人。例如，给新入职的人安排更频繁的一对一，而对已经站稳脚跟的资深成员则减少频率（前提是他们也认同这样做）。

Make temporary adjustments做临时调整

When faced with tight deadlines, you might need to reduce or skip one-on-ones temporarily to focus on hands-on work. Use this option carefully and with caution! Always set clear expectations and communicate up front about the changes.

当截止日期很紧时，你可能需要暂时减少或跳过一对一，以便专注于动手干活。请谨慎、克制地使用这个选项！务必提前讲清楚预期，并把变化提前沟通到位。

While it's normal for the frequency of your one-on-ones to evolve over time, consistency must remain the rule. Skipping a one-on-one should always be a last resort, and you should ensure it's a rare occurrence.

虽然一对一的频率会随时间演变是正常的，但"一致性"必须始终是原则。跳过一次一对一永远应该是最后手段，而且要确保这种情况很少发生。

The consistent presence of these meetings on your calendar sends a powerful message: you value your team members, you're committed to showing up for them, and you care about the relationship you're building. That reliability is what establishes trust: the foundation for everything else you'll achieve together.

这些会议稳定地出现在你的日历上，会传递一个有力的信号：你重视团队成员、你承诺为他们投入时间、你在乎正在建立的关系。正是这种可靠性建立起信任——而信任是你们日后共同成就一切的基石。

AGREE ON AGENDA AND EXPECTATIONS就议程和期望达成一致

— PDF p.109 —

For one-on-ones to work, everyone needs to know what to expect. It's up to you to set those clear expectations: what you expect from them and what they can expect from you. These meetings should feel intentional, predictable, and, most importantly, theirs.

要让一对一真正起作用，每个人都需要知道可以期待什么。这取决于你来设定清晰的期望：你对他们的期望是什么，他们又可以从你这里得到什么。这些会议应该让人感到是有意图的、可预期的，而最重要的——是属于他们的。

Start by aligning on the purpose: these meetings are about supporting them, addressing their challenges, and helping them grow. When team members own the agenda, one-on-ones become more meaningful. Encourage them to take the lead, bringing their priorities, questions, or topics to discuss. If you have something to add, let them know ahead of time. When they drive the conversation, they're more likely to come prepared and open up.

先就目的达成一致：这些会议是为了支持他们、帮他们应对挑战、助他们成长。当团队成员主导议程时，一对一会变得更有意义。鼓励他们带头，把自己优先关心的事、问题或想讨论的话题带来。如果你有想补充的内容，提前告诉他们。当他们主导对话时，他们更可能有备而来、也更愿意敞开心扉。

To ensure shared ownership:

为了确保共同主导：

Let them drive the agenda让他们主导议程

It's about their priorities, not yours. If they're unsure, guide them on what to bring to the table, but leave the floor open for their input.

谈的是他们关心的事，不是你的。如果他们不确定，可以引导他们该带些什么来，但始终把发言空间留给他们。

Focus on their concerns聚焦他们关心的事

Discuss what's top of their mind. If they ask for help, ensure they feel safe doing so.

讨论他们脑海里最紧要的事。如果他们求助，要确保他们感到这样做是安全的。

Be prepared as a backup做好备用准备

Have a few topics in mind in case they don't come with something specific that week.

心里备好几个话题，以防他们那周没带具体内容来。

Your first one-on-one is your chance to set the tone for future one-on-ones. Use it to explain the following:

你的第一次一对一，是为以后所有一对一定调的机会。用它来讲清楚以下几点：

What they can expect from you他们可以从你这里得到什么

Consistency, showing up prepared, and using this time to focus entirely on them.

保持稳定节奏、有备而来，并把这段时间完全专注在他们身上。

What you expect from them你对他们的期望

Taking ownership of the agenda, being honest about challenges, and using this space for meaningful discussions.

主动主导议程、坦诚面对挑战，并把这个空间用于有意义的讨论。

Topics of conversation对话话题

Check the section "Know What Topics to Cover" on page 94 for ideas.

参考第 94 页"了解该聊哪些话题"一节获取灵感。

Confidentiality保密性

Unless there's a serious concern that needs to be escalated for safety or ethical reasons, what's shared in your one-on-ones stays between the two of you. If there's ever something that needs to be communicated more broadly, like to a manager or HR, you'll be transparent about it and let them know beforehand. The goal is to create a space where they can speak openly without fear of unintended consequences.

除非出于安全或伦理原因需要升级上报的严重问题，否则你们一对一里谈的内容只留在你们两人之间。如果确实有需要更广范围沟通的事——比如告知经理或 HR——你会保持透明，并提前让对方知道。目标是创造一个空间，让他们可以敞开心扉，而不必担心意外的后果。

— PDF p.110 —

Here are some questions you can use:

这里有一些你可以使用的问题：

  • What do you expect from these one-on-ones?你对这些一对一有什么期望？
  • What do you expect from me as a tech lead?你希望我作为技术负责人做到什么？
  • What would make these meetings valuable for you?怎样才能让这些会议对你有价值？
  • How can I best support your work and growth?我怎样才能最好地支持你的工作和成长？
  • How do you like to prepare for these meetings?你喜欢怎样为这些会议做准备？

This alignment builds trust and ensures one-on-ones are productive. A clear structure goes a long way in building trust and consistency:

这种对齐能建立信任，并确保一对一富有成效。清晰的结构对于建立信任和一致性大有帮助：

Frequency频率

Set a regular cadence that fits the individual's needs. Some may benefit from more frequent check-ins, while others may prefer less frequent ones. Whatever frequency you agree on, make sure there is clear alignment.

设定一个符合个人需求的固定节奏。有些人可能从更频繁的碰盘中受益，另一些人则可能更喜欢不那么频繁。无论你们约定哪种频率，都要确保双方理解一致。

Calendar invites日历邀请

Make it official by sending recurring invites.

通过发送重复日历邀请，让这件事正式化。

Creative naming巧妙命名

Reduce pressure with casual names like "Weekly Sync" or "How Can I Help?"

用轻松的名字来降低压力，比如"Weekly Sync（每周同步）"或"How Can I Help?（我能帮你什么？）"。

Description会议说明

Include a short note outlining the purpose of the one-on-one and any agenda points. To keep it simple, just link to your shared one-on-one notes document instead of updating the calendar invite each time.

加一段简短说明，概述一对一的目的和议程要点。为了简单起见，可以直接链接到你们共享的一对一笔记文档，而不必每次都更新日历邀请。

Setting clear expectations from the beginning will reduce the pressure on you and the attendees that usually comes with this meeting.

从一开始就设定清晰的期望，会减轻你和与会者通常伴随这种会议而来的压力。

KNOW WHAT TOPICS TO COVER了解该聊哪些话题

One-on-ones can cover a wide range of topics, and if you're doing it right, you'll rarely run out of meaningful things to talk about. From small talk to feedback to team dynamics, each conversation is a chance to connect, clarify, and collaborate.

一对一可以涵盖广泛的话题；如果你做对了，几乎永远不会缺有意义的事情可聊。从寒暄到反馈再到团队动态，每一次对话都是一次建立联结、厘清问题、协作共事的机会。

For example, building relationships often starts with something as simple as small talk. Kicking off with "How was your weekend?" or checking in on something personal like "How's the home-buying process going?" can open the door to more meaningful conversations. You can also ask openers like "What have you been up to this week?" or follow up on something from your notes.

例如，建立关系往往从最简单的寒暄开始。用"周末过得怎么样？"开场，或者关心一下私事，比如"买房进展怎么样了？"，都能为更有意义的对话打开大门。你也可以用"这周你都在忙些什么？"这样的开场白，或者就你笔记里记的某件事跟进一下。

— PDF p.111 —

One strategy I've found effective for getting people to open up is starting with a genuine, honest answer to "How are you?" yourself. For example: "I'm really excited about a piece of work that's coming up" or "To be honest, I'm having a rough day today." Leading with openness gives permission for the other person to do the same. If all you're offering is "I'm doing OK," you're missing an opportunity to deepen that connection.

我发现一个让人敞开心扉的有效策略是：你自己先真诚、诚实地回答"你好吗？"。例如："我对即将开始的一项工作特别兴奋"，或者"说实话，我今天有点不顺"。以坦诚开场，等于允许对方也这样做。如果你给出的只是"我还行"，那就是错过了一次加深联结的机会。

Growth is another essential area. Sometimes, team members naturally bring this up: "I've been working on improving my communication skills" or "I need help getting better at X." But when they don't, it's on you to make it part of the conversation. Ask questions like "What are your goals for the next few months?" or "What areas do you want to grow in, and how can I support that?" You can also go deeper with questions such as "What are your goals for this year?," "Do you have a plan to reach them?," or "What do you need from the team or the organization to support your progress?" This helps you understand where they are now, where they want to go, and how you can help them get there. You can also follow up on goals. Ask questions like "How is that communication course going?" or "Have you had the chance to try out that new skill in a project yet?" Showing you remember and care about their growth builds trust and keeps them accountable in a supportive way.

成长是另一个必不可少的话题领域。有时团队成员会自然提起："我最近在提升沟通能力"，或者"我需要在 X 方面变得更好"。但当他们不提时，就需要你把它带进对话。问这样的问题："接下来几个月你的目标是什么？"或者"你想在哪些方面成长？我可以怎么支持你？"你也可以更深入地问："你今年的目标是什么？""你有实现它们的计划吗？""你需要团队或组织提供什么来支持你的进展？"这能帮你了解他们现在在哪里、想去哪里、以及你能怎么帮他们到达。你也可以跟进目标："那门沟通课上得怎么样了？"或者"你有没有机会在某个项目里试试那个新技能？"表现出你记得并在乎他们的成长，会建立信任，并以一种支持性的方式让他们保持对目标的投入。

Bring visibility to their work. People often don't know how much their work is valued until someone tells them. Use one-on-ones to acknowledge contributions that might otherwise go unnoticed. You might say, "I think you handled that conversation on Tuesday with the client really well." It reinforces their impact and encourages continued initiative. You can also help them find other opportunities to make their work more visible, as this is an area many engineers struggle with. Ask questions that open the door: "That was a great training on Kafka Streams you gave to the team. How would you feel about presenting it to other teams as well?" or "Have you thought about writing a short internal blog post about the debugging process you figured out last week?" Small nudges like these can build confidence and help them develop their voice beyond the immediate team.

让他们的工作被看见。人们往往不知道自己的工作有多被重视，直到有人告诉他们。利用一对一去认可那些 otherwise 可能被忽略的贡献。你可以说："我觉得你周二和客户那场对话处理得非常好。"这会强化他们的影响力，并鼓励他们继续主动。你也可以帮他们找到更多让工作被看见的机会——因为这是许多工程师都不擅长的领域。用问题打开大门："你给团队做的那场关于 Kafka Streams 的分享很棒。你觉得再给其他团队也讲一次怎么样？"或者"你有没有想过把上周自己搞定的那个调试过程写一篇简短的内部博客？"这样小小的推动，能建立信心，帮他们在团队之外发展出自己的话语权。

Feedback often fits naturally into one-on-ones. If there's something you've been meaning to share but haven't had the chance, this is the perfect time, though don't make the mistake of relying solely on these meetings for feedback. And it goes both ways. Use this time to ask for feedback from them: "How do you think I handled that situation?" or "What could I have done better in this morning's presentation?"

反馈在一对一里往往来得很自然。如果你一直想分享点什么却没找到机会，这正是时候——但不要犯这个错误：把反馈完全寄托在这些会议上。而且反馈是双向的。利用这段时间向他们征求反馈："你觉得我处理那件事的方式怎么样？"或者"今天早上的汇报，我哪里本可以做得更好？"

— PDF p.112 —

Team dynamics can also come into focus during these discussions. Ask open-ended questions like "What do you think we need more of in the team?" or "What's something you think we could do better?" These questions often reveal underlying issues or areas for improvement you might not have seen otherwise, and they open the door to something even deeper.

团队动态也会在这些讨论中成为焦点。问一些开放式问题，比如"你觉得我们团队还需要多一点什么？"或者"你觉得有什么我们可以做得更好？"这些问题往往能揭示出你平时看不到的深层问题或改进空间，并为更深入的东西打开大门。

Use one-on-ones as a regular safety check. Beyond surfacing ideas and team improvements, these conversations are a powerful tool for gauging how safe and supported your team members feel. You can start by asking, "How are you feeling about the team these days?" or "Is anything making your day-to-day harder than it needs to be?" These kinds of questions help you monitor psychological safety and create a space where people know it's OK to raise concerns, big or small, before they become blockers.

把一对一当作定期的安全体检。除了暴露想法和团队改进点之外，这些对话还是衡量团队成员感到多安全、多被支持的有力工具。你可以这样开场："你最近对团队感觉怎么样？"或者"有没有什么事让你的日常工作比本来更艰难？"这类问题帮你监测心理安全，并创造一个空间，让大家知道：无论大小顾虑，在它们变成拦路石之前都可以提出来。

Be mindful of changes in tone, energy, or participation. If someone who's usually engaged seems withdrawn or vague, gently check in. Questions like "You seem quieter than usual; how are things going?" can open the door for honest conversations that might otherwise be missed.

留意语气、精力或参与度的变化。如果一个平时很投入的人显得退缩或含糊，温和地问一问。像"你今天好像比平时安静；最近怎么样？"这样的问题，能开启原本可能被错过的诚实对话。

To build reflection into your one-on-ones, consider incorporating a few lightweight, recurring questions. These can help people pause and take stock of their week while giving you insights into their mindset and workload. Try asking:

要把反思融入一对一，可以考虑加入几个轻量、反复出现的问题。它们能帮大家停下来盘点自己这一周，同时让你了解他们的心态和工作量。可以试试问：

  • What's something you learned this week?这周你学到了什么？
  • What's one thing that went well?有哪件事进展顺利？
  • What's been challenging you recently?最近有什么让你感到有挑战的事？

Make space for wins. One-on-ones are a great opportunity to celebrate progress, even the small stuff. Asking questions like "What's something you're proud of from the last sprint?" or "Has anyone on the team helped you out recently in a way that stood out?" helps surface moments of success and appreciation. These quick reflections can be energizing and often trigger further conversations about motivation and what's working well in the team.

为"小胜"留出空间。一对一是庆祝进展的好机会——哪怕是很小的进展。问"上个冲刺你有什么值得骄傲的事？"或者"最近团队里有没有谁帮到你，让你印象特别深？"这类问题，能让成功和被感谢的时刻浮现出来。这些简短的反思能给人能量，还常常引发关于动力、关于团队里什么运转良好的进一步对话。

Pay attention to throwaway comments or subtle hesitations. "I've been dealing with some weird bugs" might just be a vent, or it might signal a larger problem worth digging into. One-on-ones are a great space to gently explore these threads.

留意那些随口一提的评论或微妙的迟疑。"我最近一直在搞一些奇怪的 bug"可能只是抱怨一下，也可能指向一个值得深挖的更大问题。一对一正是温和地梳理这些线索的好地方。

Then there are the inevitable questions and worries that people bring. They might ask, "I heard there's going to be some restructuring. How will that affect us?" These moments are your chance to calm nerves, provide clarity, or at least show empathy when you don't have all the answers yet.

还有人们不可避免会带来的疑问和担忧。他们可能会问："我听说要架构调整了。那会怎么影响我们？"这种时刻就是你的机会：去安抚情绪、讲清情况，或者在你还没有全部答案时，至少表达共情。

— PDF p.113 —

The most valuable one-on-ones tend to revisit a mix of themes: connection, growth, feedback, team health, and reflection. You don't need to cover everything every time, but having this mental map helps keep conversations balanced over time.

最有价值的一对一，往往会反复回到一组主题：联结、成长、反馈、团队健康和反思。你不需要每次都把所有话题覆盖到，但心里有这张地图，能帮你让对话在时间上保持平衡。

Ultimately, one-on-ones are there to support them in whatever way they need. They should feel like they own the meeting and you're there as a partner in their growth.

归根到底，一对一是为了以他们需要的任何方式支持他们。他们应该感觉这场会是自己的，而你是他们成长路上的伙伴。

CREATE A SAFE SPACE营造安全空间

Creating a safe space in your one-on-ones is essential. Without it, meaningful conversations can't happen, and the real value of these meetings is lost.

在一对一里营造安全空间至关重要。没有它，有意义的对话就无法发生，这些会议的真正价值也就荡然无存。

One way to build this kind of space is to drop the formality. When I was working in an office, I'd sometimes invite people for a coffee outside during our one-on-one time, my treat. We'd take a short walk to a nearby café, chat casually on the way, and then settle on a bench in the park for a more thoughtful conversation. People loved it. That shift in environment and tone, stepping away from desks and screens, helped lower walls and made it easier to connect on a more human level. So if you have the chance to meet people face-to-face, take it! Even in a hybrid setup, I would plan a day at the office with my team and schedule my one-on-ones in person whenever possible. These moments of presence and connection often go a long way in building trust.

营造这种空间的一个方法，就是放下正式感。当我还在办公室上班时，有时会趁一对一的时间请人出去喝杯咖啡——我请客。我们会走到附近的咖啡馆，路上随便聊聊，然后在公园的长椅上坐下来，进行一次更深入的谈话。大家都很喜欢。这种环境和氛围的切换——离开工位和屏幕——帮人卸下防备，让人与人之间更容易建立联结。所以如果你有机会面对面见人，一定要抓住！即使是混合办公，我也会安排和团队一起到办公室的日子，并尽可能当面进行一对一。这些同在现场、彼此联结的时刻，对建立信任往往大有帮助。

The next step is how you show up in these conversations. One simple strategy I use to set the tone is starting with a genuine answer to "How are you?" Instead of a surface-level response, I'll share something real: "I'm feeling excited about this new project" or "I've had a tough morning because…" This honesty invites them to open up, showing that it's OK to be authentic in this space. If you want people to open up, you have to open up first. Vulnerability is contagious.

下一步，是你在这些对话里以什么样的状态出现。我用来定调的一个简单策略，就是先用真诚的方式回答"你好吗？"。我不会给出表面的回应，而是分享一些真实的东西："这个新项目让我挺兴奋"，或者"我今天早上过得不太顺，因为……"。这种坦诚会邀请对方也敞开心扉，让他们看到：在这个空间里做真实的自己是可以的。如果你想让别人敞开心扉，你得先敞开心扉。脆弱是会传染的。

I once mentioned in a one-on-one with a team member that I was feeling overwhelmed adjusting to a new process we were trialing. She immediately opened up about how she'd also been struggling but didn't want to seem negative. That moment turned our dynamic: it moved the conversation from polite check-ins to a more open and honest relationship. It reminded both of us that we weren't alone in navigating challenges.

有一次，我在和一位团队成员的一对一里提到，我正在适应一个我们试用的新流程，感到有点应接不暇。她立刻敞开心扉，说她其实也一直很吃力，只是不想显得负面。那一刻改变了我们之间的互动：对话从客气的例行碰盘，变成了更坦诚、更真实的关系。它也提醒我们俩：在应对挑战这件事上，我们并不孤单。

By being honest about your thoughts and feelings, you make it easier for the other person to do the same.

通过坦诚自己的想法和感受，你让对方也更容易这样做。

Listening is the most powerful tool you have for building trust and creating a safe space. It's not just about hearing words; it's about understanding the person in front of you. Truly listening helps you develop empathy by seeing things from their perspective. When you do this, you connect on a deeper level and gain insight into what drives and challenges them.

倾听是你建立信任、营造安全空间最有力的工具。它不只是听见话语；更是理解你面前这个人。真正的倾听帮你站在他们的视角看问题，从而培养共情。当你这样做时，你们会在更深的层面建立联结，并洞察到是什么在驱动他们、又是什么在困扰他们。

— PDF p.114 —

Here's how to make your listening count:

以下是让你的倾听真正有效的方法：

Focus on the speaker专注于说话者

One of the simplest yet most powerful shifts you can make is reminding yourself: this is not about me. I even keep a sticky note on my monitor that says exactly that. To really focus, you need to eliminate distractions: turn off notifications, put your phone away, and be fully present. Especially while working remotely, I found this harder to manage. So now, before one-on-ones or important conversations, I turn on "Do Not Disturb," switch to full-screen mode, and keep a notebook nearby to offload distracting thoughts.

你能做的最简单却最有力的一个转变，就是提醒自己：这不是关于我。我甚至在显示器上贴了一张便签，上面就写着这句话。要真正专注，你需要消除干扰：关掉通知、把手机收起来、全情投入。尤其是远程办公时，我发现这更难做到。所以现在，在一对一或重要对话之前，我会打开"勿扰模式"、切到全屏，并在旁边放一个笔记本，用来把脑子里飘走的念头记下来。

Embrace silence接纳沉默

If you want to listen more, you have to talk less. Early in my career, I felt the need to fill every silence or always have the last word. But I realized I was unintentionally crowding out others' contributions. Not every one-on-one will flow effortlessly, especially early on or with more introverted team members, and that's OK. Silence can feel awkward, but it's a crucial part of the conversation. It gives people space to gather their thoughts and build the courage to bring up something difficult.

如果你想多倾听，就必须少说话。在我职业生涯早期，我总想填满每一段沉默，或者总要抢最后一句话。但我意识到，自己在不知不觉中挤占了别人发言的空间。不是每一场一对一都会流畅自然，尤其是早期、或者面对更内向的团队成员时，这都很正常。沉默可能让人尴尬，但它是对话中至关重要的一部分。它给人空间整理思路、鼓起勇气去提起那些难以启齿的事。

To change my habits, I started defaulting to mute during remote meetings to give others room. One time, I forgot I was muted and started talking, only to realize the team had continued the discussion without me. They were doing just fine. That moment reminded me: my job isn't to steer every conversation but to create space for others to contribute.

为了改变习惯，我在远程会议里开始默认静音，好给别人留出空间。有一次，我忘了自己静音就开口说话，结果才发现团队早就在没有我的情况下继续讨论了。他们进行得好好的。那一刻提醒了我：我的工作不是掌舵每一场对话，而是为别人创造贡献的空间。

Over time, I also learned to embrace silence instead of rushing to fill it. One trick that helped: count to 39 in your head. Most of the time, someone speaks up long before you finish counting, but even if they don't, that pause often leads to richer contributions than if you'd jumped in too quickly. You can say "Take your time" or simply sit with the quiet for a moment. Creating comfort with pauses helps make one-on-ones feel safer and more thoughtful.

久而久之，我也学会了接纳沉默，而不是急着去填满它。一个有用的小技巧：在心里数到 39。大多数时候，别人早在你数完之前就开口了；但即便没有，那个停顿也往往比你过早插话带来更丰富的内容。你可以说"慢慢来"，或者就和这份安静共处一会儿。学会与停顿相处，能让一对一感觉更安全、更有思考深度。

— PDF p.115 —

Reflect and seek feedback复述并寻求反馈

Reflecting back what you've heard is one of the most powerful ways to show you're truly listening. After someone shares something important, take a moment to summarize and check if you've understood correctly: "So what I'm hearing is that you feel your ideas aren't fully considered during technical discussions because the group often leans toward a different approach. Does that sound right?" This kind of reflection not only helps clarify their message; it also shows that you're making an effort to truly understand them.

把你听到的内容复述回去，是展示你在真正倾听的最有力方式之一。当别人分享了重要的事之后，花一点时间总结一下，确认自己理解得对不对："所以我听到的是：你觉得在技术讨论中，你的想法没有被充分考虑，因为大家往往倾向于另一种做法。是这样吗？"这种复述不仅帮对方把意思讲清楚，也表明你在努力真正理解他们。

But listening doesn't stop when the conversation ends. Becoming a better listener takes deliberate practice. After key conversations, especially one-on-ones or feedback sessions, I set aside 15 minutes to reflect. How well did I listen, on a scale from 1 to 10? Where did I drift off and why? Did I interrupt? I also make a point of asking for feedback directly, with questions like "What's one thing I could do to make you feel more heard?" or "How do you think I handle conversations when we disagree?" Over time, the answers to these questions have helped me refine not just how I listen, but how I lead.

但倾听并不随着对话结束而停止。成为更好的倾听者需要刻意练习。在重要对话之后——尤其是一对一或反馈会谈之后——我会留出 15 分钟反思。如果 1 到 10 分，我倾听得有多好？我什么时候走神了？为什么？我有没有打断别人？我也会特意直接征求反馈，问这样的问题："我可以做哪一件事，让你感觉自己被更好地倾听？"或者"你觉得我们意见不一致时，我处理对话的方式怎么样？"久而久之，这些问题的答案不仅帮我改进了倾听方式，也改进了我的领导方式。

Ask clarifying questions提出澄清性问题

Use open-ended questions to dig deeper and gain more context. For example, "Can you tell me more about why you feel that way?" or "What do you think would help in that situation?" These questions encourage them to share more while keeping the focus on their experience.

用开放式问题来深入挖掘、获取更多背景。例如："你能多说说为什么会有这种感觉吗？"或者"你觉得在那种情况下，什么会有帮助？"这些问题鼓励对方分享更多，同时把焦点保持在他们的经历上。

These strategies help you create space for open, honest dialogue, but they work only if you can stay present in emotionally charged moments too.

这些策略帮你为坦诚对话创造空间，但前提是你在情绪激动的时刻也能保持在场。

If a team member comes into a one-on-one clearly frustrated, venting about a difficult situation with the team or a recent meeting, your job isn't to fix it right away. In those moments, the most supportive thing you can do is simply stay with them. Don't interrupt, don't offer solutions, and don't jump to defend yourself if you feel the frustration is aimed your way. Just stay present and let them finish. I know how hard this can be; I've been there. It can feel like they'll never stop, like you need to respond. But I promise: they always stop. And if you've truly been listening, they'll know.

如果一位团队成员带着明显的沮丧走进一对一，倾诉着团队里的某个难题或最近一次会议的糟心经历，你的工作不是立刻去解决它。在那些时刻，你能做的最有支持性的事，就是单纯地陪着他们。不要打断、不要给解决方案，如果你觉得那股情绪是冲着你来的，也不要急着为自己辩护。就只是在场，让他们说完。我知道这有多难；我经历过。那感觉就像他们永远停不下来，你必须立刻回应。但我保证：他们总会停下来的。而如果你真的在听，他们会知道的。

At the end of these moments, I often just take a breath and say, "I hear you. I'm sorry this has been so hard. What would you like me to do about it?" Sometimes, their response is "Nothing; I just needed to get it off my chest." That's the point: the sharing is for them, not for you. And asking this simple question helps you clarify their needs instead of guessing. Worst case? They tell you exactly what they want you to do, and you can decide how to act on it. But more often than not, the act of listening is the support they needed all along.

在这些时刻的末尾，我通常只是吸一口气，然后说："我听到了。很抱歉这让你这么难受。关于这件事，你希望我做什么？"有时候他们的回答是："不用做什么；我只是想把它倒出来。"这才是重点：倾诉是为了他们，不是为了你。而问这个简单的问题，帮你厘清他们的需要，而不是去猜。最坏的情况是什么？他们清楚地告诉你希望你做什么，然后你可以决定如何行动。但更多时候，倾听本身就是他们一直以来需要的支持。

— PDF p.116 —

The openness people show in one-on-ones is a good measure of team safety. Hesitation, tension, or frustration might signal deeper issues. These insights can help you address problems early and build a safer, more collaborative team environment.

人们在一对一里展现出的开放程度，是衡量团队安全感的一把好尺子。迟疑、紧张或沮丧，都可能暗示更深层的问题。这些洞察能帮你及早处理问题，构建一个更安全、更协作的团队环境。

TRACK CONVERSATIONS记录对话内容

One-on-ones aren't isolated chats; they're part of a long, ongoing conversation. Growth doesn't happen overnight, and some challenges can't be solved in a single meeting. Consistency and follow-up are key to making these meetings impactful, and the only way to do it right is to track what's being discussed.

一对一不是孤立的闲聊；它是一场漫长、持续对话的一部分。成长不会一夜发生，有些挑战也无法在一次会议里解决。一致性和跟进是让这些会议产生影响的关键，而把这件事做对的唯一方法，就是记录下讨论了什么。

I used to keep an online note for each team member, dedicating a few minutes after every one-on-one to jot down key points: what we discussed, action items, and topics to revisit. During these meetings, I kept a notebook handy for capturing high-level ideas, allowing me to stay present. I tracked personal details like "getting a dog" or "new hobby," professional milestones or projects they were tackling, and follow-ups on development goals or challenges for future conversations.

我过去会为每位团队成员建一份在线笔记，每次一对一后花几分钟记下要点：我们谈了什么、待办事项、以及以后要回顾的话题。开会时，我手边放一个笔记本，用来记下高层的想法，这样我就能保持在场。我会记下一些个人细节，比如"要养一只狗"或"新爱好"，记下他们正在推进的职业里程碑或项目，以及留给以后对话跟进的成长目标或挑战。

Tip: Having a shared file for one-on-ones was a game-changer. It allowed team members to add their agenda in advance and track action items together, ensuring accountability on both sides.

提示：为一对一建一份共享文档，效果是颠覆性的。它让团队成员可以提前添加自己的议程，并一起跟踪待办事项，从而确保双方都有问责。

Even with a shared document, I kept my personal notes for extra context. These were for things like remembering personal details, feedback I wanted to circle back on, or insights I'd want to bring up later. This combination of shared tracking and private notes helped me show up prepared and keep the continuity of our conversations.

即便有了共享文档，我仍然保留自己的私人笔记作为额外背景。它们用来记一些个人细节、我想回头再提的反馈、或者以后想拿来聊的洞察。共享记录加私人笔记的这种组合，帮我每次都有备而来，并维持了对话的连贯性。

Tracking also strengthens your follow-up game. When someone raises a concern, use your notes to keep track of actions you need to take and circle back. Give them an update, even if the outcome isn't ideal or you couldn't take action. Just closing the loop builds trust and reinforces the message: I heard you, and I followed through. It shows your team they can rely on you and that their concerns won't disappear into the void.

记录还能强化你的跟进能力。当有人提出顾虑时，用笔记跟踪你需要采取的行动，然后回头反馈。给他们一个进展更新，哪怕结果不理想、或者你没能采取行动。仅仅是把闭环走完，就能建立信任，并强化这个信号：我听到了你的话，而且我跟进到底了。这让团队知道他们可以依靠你，他们的顾虑不会石沉大海。

Tracking conversations shows your team that their time is valuable and that you're invested in their growth. It's also an opportunity to ask simple but powerful questions: "How can I make your life easier?" These small actions build trust and make sure your one-on-ones aren't just chats but actually help move things forward.

记录对话向团队表明：他们的时间很宝贵，你真心投入在他们的成长上。这也是一个提出简单却有力的问题的机会："我怎么做能让你的工作轻松一点？"这些小小的行动积累起信任，确保你的一对一不只是聊天，而是真的在推动事情前进。

— PDF p.117 —

AVOID COMMON ONE-ON-ONE PITFALLS避开常见的一对一沟通误区

One-on-ones are powerful but only if you treat them with the care they deserve. Unfortunately, some of the biggest mistakes aren't about what you don't do but about what you do without realizing the impact.

一对一是强大的工具，但前提是你以它们应得的用心来对待。不幸的是，一些最大的错误不在于你没做什么，而在于你做了、却没有意识到其影响。

For example, showing up distracted, checking your phone, replying to Slack messages, or looking at another screen signals that this meeting isn't your priority. Over time, that erodes trust. The same goes for turning these sessions into complaint outlets. Sharing your challenges is fine, but when one-on-ones become a space for you to vent about other team members, stakeholders, or leadership, it puts your report in an uncomfortable position and undermines psychological safety.

例如，开会时分心、看手机、回 Slack 消息、或者盯着另一个屏幕，都在传递一个信号：这场会不是你的优先事项。久而久之，这会侵蚀信任。把这些会谈变成抱怨出口也是一样。分享你自己的挑战没问题，但当一对一变成你吐槽其他团队成员、干系人或领导层的空间时，就会让你的下属处于不舒服的境地，并破坏心理安全。

Another common pitfall: dismissing concerns as "just complaining." What you hear as a rant might actually be a sign of deeper friction or misalignment. As a tech lead, your job is to listen with curiosity and look for patterns or problems behind the words, even if they're not expressed perfectly.

另一个常见误区：把别人的顾虑当成"只是抱怨"而不屑一顾。你听上去像在发牢骚的话，实际上可能是更深层摩擦或不一致的信号。作为技术负责人，你的工作是带着好奇心倾听，在话语背后寻找模式或问题，哪怕对方表达得并不完美。

Also be mindful of dominating the conversation with your own updates or personal stories. A common trap is thinking you're being relatable by sharing too much about your own situation, especially when a team member is vulnerable. For example, they share something they're struggling with, and your instinct is to jump in with a similar story of your own. While well-intended, this can make the conversation about you, rather than helping them feel seen and supported.

还要注意不要用你自己的进展或个人故事主导对话。一个常见的陷阱是：以为分享太多自己的处境就能拉近距离，尤其是在团队成员敞开心扉时。例如，他们分享自己正在挣扎的事，你的本能反应是插入一个自己的类似故事。虽然出发点是好的，但这会把对话变成关于你，而不是帮他们感到被看见、被支持。

If you find yourself doing most of the talking, pause and reflect: Is it because you're trying to fill silence? Are you uncomfortable with their discomfort? Are you unsure what to say, so you're defaulting to what's easy for you? These are all normal instincts, but they shift the focus away from the person who needs you to listen most.

如果你发现自己说了大部分话，停下来反思一下：是因为你想填补沉默吗？是因为你对他们的不适感感到不自在吗？是因为你不知道该说什么，所以退回到自己最容易说的东西上吗？这些都是正常的本能反应，但它们把焦点从那个最需要你倾听的人身上移开了。

One helpful self-check: after every one-on-one, ask yourself, "Did I walk away understanding more about them than they learned about me?" If not, it might be time to rebalance how you're using that time.

一个有用的自我检查：每次一对一结束后，问自己："我离开时对他们的了解，是否多过他们对我的了解？"如果不是，也许是时候重新平衡你使用这段时间的方式了。

Finally, never underestimate the damage of inaction. If someone brings up an issue and you nod through it but do nothing, or forget it entirely, it sends a clear message: this space doesn't lead anywhere. When that happens enough times, people stop bringing things up.

最后，永远不要低估不作为的破坏力。如果有人提出一个问题，你点头应承却什么都不做，或者干脆忘掉，那传递出的信号很清楚：这个空间不会通向任何地方。这种事发生足够多次后，人们就不再提了。

— PDF p.118 —

Being aware of the common pitfalls helps you avoid the slow erosion of safety and connection.

意识到这些常见误区，能帮你避免安全与联结被慢慢侵蚀。

Overcoming Common Challenges克服常见挑战

One-on-ones can be incredibly impactful when done well, but they often come with challenges that can derail their value. As a tech lead, you may encounter recurring issues like struggling to find meaningful topics to discuss, sessions being canceled too often, or feeling like you have to solve everyone's problems. In this section, I'll explore these common roadblocks and provide actionable strategies to overcome them, so your one-on-ones can become productive, consistent, and meaningful conversations that benefit both you and your team.

一对一如果做得好，可以产生巨大的影响，但它们常常伴随一些挑战，可能让价值脱轨。作为技术负责人，你可能会反复遇到这类问题：找不到有意义的话题可聊、会谈被过于频繁地取消、或者感觉自己必须解决每个人的问题。在本节中，我会探讨这些常见路障，并提供可落地的应对策略，让你的一对一变成高效、稳定、有意义的对话，让你和团队都受益。

NOTHING TO TALK ABOUT没什么可聊的

Troubleshooting disengagement starts with identifying the root cause. Is it a team-wide issue, or is it just one individual?

排查"不投入"要从找到根因开始。这是整个团队的问题，还是某一个人的问题？

If it's the whole team, the problem might be you. This often happens when there's a gap in how you've set up or are running your one-on-ones.

如果是整个团队，问题可能出在你身上。这通常发生在你安排或开展一对一的方式有欠缺时。

We can use Table 4-2 to troubleshoot.

我们可以用表 4-2 来排查。

Table 4-2. Common challenges that arise on one-on-ones and suggested solutions

表 4-2. 一对一沟通中常见的挑战与建议对策

Challenge / 挑战Suggestion / 建议
Team members seem disengaged in one-on-ones.团队成员在一对一沟通中似乎不投入。Start by having an explicit conversation in the one-on-one. Ask for their feedback on how valuable they find these meetings and what you might do to improve them. Also, ensure your one-on-ones are consistent. Sporadic meetings or skipped sessions signal they're not a priority, which can lead to disengagement.先在一对一里直接谈一谈。征求他们对这些会议价值的反馈，以及你可以做些什么来改进。同时，确保一对一保持规律。不定期的会议或被跳过的会谈会传递出"不受重视"的信号，进而导致不投入。
Meetings feel unproductive and scattered.会议显得低效且散乱。Encourage them to come up with an agenda beforehand. Align on the purpose and value of these sessions to ensure both parties are prepared and engaged.鼓励他们提前准备议程。就这些会议的目的和价值达成一致，确保双方都有准备、有参与。
Team members rarely bring up meaningful topics.团队成员很少提出有意义的话题。Discuss potential topics in advance. Make it clear what's fair game for discussion, so they feel comfortable bringing up points that matter.提前讨论可能的话题。明确哪些内容都可以谈，让他们能自在地提出真正重要的问题。
The team is holding back or not sharing openly.团队有所保留、不愿敞开心扉。Build trust by creating a safe space for conversations. If this persists, revisit strategies in the section "How to Build Strong Relationships" on page 62 to address trust issues.通过营造安全的对话空间来建立信任。如果这种情况持续存在，回到第 62 页"如何建立牢固的关系"一节中的策略来解决信任问题。
Conversations feel stagnant and repetitive.对话显得停滞、重复。Follow up on action items and progress from previous meetings. Show continuity and commitment by revisiting prior discussions and tracking outcomes.跟进上次会议的待办事项和进展。通过回顾之前的讨论并跟踪结果，体现连贯性和投入度。

Addressing these challenges will help pinpoint where to start addressing the issue.

应对这些挑战，能帮你准确定位从哪里入手解决问题。

— PDF p.119 —

If it's an individual, dig deeper. Disengagement from one team member might hint at personal challenges or demotivation. I once had a team member bring no topics for weeks. When I finally asked about it, I found out she was frustrated about missing out on a project she really wanted to be involved with. We discussed other opportunities that excited her, and the problem vanished.

如果是某一个人，就往深处挖。某一位团队成员的不投入，可能暗示着个人的困难或动力不足。我曾经有一位团队成员连续几周都不带话题来。当我终于问起时，发现她因为错过了一个自己很想参与的项目而沮丧。我们聊了聊其他能让她兴奋的机会，问题就消失了。

Even though it's their responsibility to bring topics, your team members might struggle, especially early on. Here's how you can help:

虽然带话题来是他们的责任，但你的团队成员可能会觉得困难，尤其是早期。以下是你可以帮忙的方式：

Track everything记录一切

Keep notes on what they're doing well, areas for improvement, personal updates, and team dynamics. These observations can trigger meaningful conversations.

记录他们做得好的地方、待改进的地方、个人近况以及团队动态。这些观察能触发有意义的对话。

Prepare prompts准备引导话题

If your team member struggles to bring up topics, have a few open-ended questions ready to trigger conversation. You can find a more complete list of ideas and question types in the section "Know What Topics to Cover" on page 94.

如果你的团队成员不擅长提出话题，就准备好几个开放式问题来引导对话。更完整的思路和问题类型清单，见第 94 页"了解该聊哪些话题"一节。

If a team member consistently shows up without topics, acknowledge it directly: "I've noticed you've been quiet in recent one-on-ones. Is there something on your mind, or is it just me?" This can lead to unexpected insights and opens the door to reminding them about the value of these meetings.

如果某位团队成员一直不带话题来，直接点出来："我注意到你最近几次一对一都比较安静。是有什么心事吗，还是只是我多想了？"这可能带来意想不到的洞察，并为提醒他们这些会议的价值打开大门。

In my experience, when someone says they have "nothing to talk about," it's rarely the whole truth. It's usually a signal that something deeper needs attention. Addressing the root cause is how you turn disengagement into meaningful conversations.

以我的经验，当有人说"没什么可聊的"时，这很少是全部真相。它通常是一个信号：有更深层的东西需要被关注。找到并解决根因，你才能把不投入变成有意义的对话。

GROUND RULES ARE NOT RESPECTED基本规则未被遵守

At the start of your one-on-ones, you and your team members agree on the rules and commit to making these meetings valuable.

在一对一刚开始时，你和团队成员会就规则达成一致，并承诺让这些会议有价值。

When things start to slip, it all comes down to reiterating those expectations and recalibrating together. Here are a few common issues that can arise, along with some ways to address them:

当情况开始走样，关键就在于重申那些期望、一起重新校准。以下是一些可能出现的常见问题，以及应对方式：

Lack of meaningful topics缺乏有意义的话题

If team members rely on you to guide discussions, address it head-on: "For the past few weeks, we haven't had much to discuss in our one-on-ones. Why do you think that is?" Remind them of the purpose: "This space is for you to bring up concerns and questions or focus on your growth. How can I support you in using it better?"

如果团队成员依赖你来引导讨论，就正面谈这件事："过去几周，我们的一对一没什么可聊的。你觉得这是为什么？"提醒他们这个空间的目的："这个空间是给你提顾虑、提问题，或者专注于自己成长用的。我怎样才能支持你更好地使用它？"

You can also share your own experience to build trust and normalize their hesitation. For example: "I remember a period when I was having one-on-ones with my own manager and I didn't bring up much beyond surface-level updates. I didn't realize it was OK to talk about the things I was unsure about, like whether I was growing fast enough or whether I should speak up more in meetings. Once I brought it up, it completely changed how useful those conversations became for me."

你也可以分享自己的经历来建立信任，让他们的迟疑显得正常。例如："我记得有段时间，我和自己经理做一对一时，除了表面的进展汇报之外，也没提什么。我当时没意识到，那些我拿不准的事——比如我成长得够不够快、我在会议里是不是该更主动发言——都是可以聊的。一旦我把它们提出来，那些对话对我的价值完全变了。"

— PDF p.120 —

Frequent cancellations频繁取消

Frequent cancellations suggest these meetings aren't being prioritized. Approach the issue with curiosity rather than frustration: "I've noticed you've canceled a few of our one-on-ones recently. Why is that?" or "How can we adjust to make these meetings more valuable and ensure they fit into your schedule?" Reiterating the importance of consistency and the value these sessions provide can help reset their commitment.

频繁取消说明这些会议没有被排在优先位置。带着好奇而不是沮丧去处理："我注意到你最近取消了好几次一对一。是为什么呢？"或者"我们怎么调整一下，能让这些会议更有价值、也更契合你的日程？"重申一致性的重要性以及这些会谈带来的价值，能帮他们重新建立承诺。

Sometimes cancellations are due to pressures outside their control, caused by things like organizational changes, shifting priorities, or overloaded calendars. If it becomes a pattern, consider digging deeper: Is there a bigger issue at play? Are they being pulled in too many directions by stakeholders or leaders? If so, see how you can help, whether that's advocating on their behalf, adjusting expectations, or surfacing the problem more broadly. Repeated cancellations may be a symptom of something larger, and addressing it directly shows leadership and care.

有时取消是因为他们无法控制的压力，比如组织变动、优先级转移，或者日程过载。如果这成了一种模式，可以考虑往深处挖：背后是不是有更大的问题？他们是不是被干系人或领导拉扯到太多方向上？如果是，看看你能怎么帮——替他们发声、调整期望，或者把问题更广泛地暴露出来。反复取消可能是更大问题的征兆，直接面对它，体现的是领导力和关怀。

Hesitation to voice concerns不愿表达顾虑

If team members aren't using their one-on-ones to voice concerns or challenges, it might signal a lack of trust or hesitation. Create a safe space by reminding them: "This is your time to discuss anything on your mind, whether it's something you're excited about or something that's worrying you. If there's anything holding you back from bringing these up, let's figure out how we can address it together." Reiterate that confidentiality is part of how one-on-ones work. You can say something like "Unless something poses a serious risk or requires escalation, what we discuss here stays between us." Making this expectation explicit can go a long way in helping team members feel safe enough to open up.

如果团队成员没有利用一对一来表达顾虑或挑战，可能意味着缺乏信任或有所迟疑。通过提醒他们来营造安全空间："这是属于你的时间，你可以聊任何你心里的事——无论是让你兴奋的事，还是让你担心的事。如果有什么让你不敢提出来，我们一起看看怎么解决。"重申保密性是一对一运行方式的一部分。你可以这样说："除非某件事构成严重风险或需要升级上报，否则我们在这里谈的内容只留在我们两人之间。"把这个期望讲明，能大大帮团队成员感到足够安全而敞开心扉。

— PDF p.121 —

The system works only if both of you stick to the process. These rules aren't just about their responsibilities; they apply to you, too. Let them know they can hold you accountable as well: "If I'm late, cancel too often, or don't follow through on what I promised, I want you to call me out on it. The system works only if we both stick to it." Even better, be proactive. If you slip, missing a meeting or coming unprepared, own it before they have to. Modeling accountability builds trust faster than asking for it.

这套机制只有在你们双方都遵守流程时才有效。这些规则不只关乎他们的责任；同样适用于你。让他们知道，他们也可以让你负责："如果我迟到、取消得太频繁、或者没有兑现承诺，我希望你直接指出来。这套机制只有在我们双方都遵守时才成立。"更好的是，主动一点。如果你自己掉了链子——比如错过一次会议或者毫无准备就来——在他们开口之前先承认。以身作则地承担责任，比口头要求问责更快建立信任。

By holding each other accountable to the ground rules you've agreed on, you ensure that these one-on-ones stay valuable, intentional, and productive over the long term.

通过按照你们约定的基本规则互相问责，你能确保这些一对一在长期里始终保持有价值、有意图、有成效。

FEELING PRESSURE TO SOLVE PROBLEMS感到必须解决所有问题的压力

As a tech lead, it's easy to feel like you need to solve every problem that comes your way. The team looks to you for guidance, but you are not responsible for solving everything. Your role is to point people in the right direction, not to fix everything yourself.

作为技术负责人，你很容易觉得自己需要解决摆在面前的每一个问题。团队指望你给出方向，但你并不负责解决所有事。你的角色是把人指向正确的方向，而不是自己把一切都修好。

An effective tech lead listens, empathizes, and supports but does not try to fix every issue. You are not supposed to! Trying to carry the weight of everyone's challenges will not only burn you out but will also prevent your team from growing.

一位高效的技术负责人倾听、共情、支持，但不会试图解决每一个问题。你本来就不该这么做！试图扛住每个人的挑战，不仅会把你自己耗竭，也会阻碍团队成长。

Instead of jumping in with solutions, think of yourself as a guide, and use the following approaches:

与其跳进去给解决方案，不如把自己当成向导，使用以下方式：

Coach教练式引导

Use powerful questions to help them find their own solutions. One way to start is by simply asking, "What do you need from me right now?" They may just want a sounding board, not a solution. Asking this up front helps you calibrate your support and shows that you're there to meet them where they are.

用有力的问题帮他们找到自己的答案。一个开场的方式就是直接问："你现在需要我做什么？"他们可能只是需要一个倾诉的对象，而不是一个解决方案。先问这个问题，能帮你校准支持的方式，也表明你会根据他们当下的状态来配合。

If they say they'd like your help figuring it out, then follow up with prompts like "What do you think might work here?" or "How would you approach this if you had no constraints?" These kinds of questions encourage ownership and growth while still making them feel supported.

如果他们说希望你帮着一起理清，那就接着引导："你觉得在这里什么办法可能行得通？"或者"如果没有任何约束，你会怎么处理这件事？"这类问题鼓励主人翁意识和成长，同时仍让他们感到被支持。

Delegate授权他人

Recognize when someone else is better positioned to help. If it's a technical issue, loop in a subject matter expert. If they're looking for career guidance, suggest connecting with a mentor. Delegating wisely extends your impact without stretching yourself too thin.

识别什么时候别人更适合来帮忙。如果是技术问题，就把领域专家拉进来。如果他们在寻求职业指导，就建议他们去找一位导师。明智地授权能扩大你的影响力，而不会把自己摊得太薄。

— PDF p.122 —

Refer转介资源

If the issue is personal or sensitive and falls outside your expertise, gently point them to the right resources. Be familiar with what's available, like employee assistance programs, mental health services, or HR contacts, so you can guide them effectively when the situation calls for professional support.

如果问题是个人的或敏感的，并且超出了你的专业范围，温和地把他们引向合适的资源。熟悉手头有哪些可用资源，比如员工帮助计划、心理健康服务或 HR 联系方式，这样当情况需要专业支持时，你能有效地引导他们。

It's helpful to show empathy, as long as you also hold clear boundaries. Not every problem brought to you will, or should, be yours to solve. If a team member expects you to fix something for them, you can respond with "I understand this is challenging, but let's explore how you can tackle it. How can I support you in finding a solution?" This approach shifts the responsibility back to them, empowering them to grow and take ownership of their challenges.

表达共情是有帮助的，前提是你同时守住清晰的边界。不是每一个带到你面前的问题都该由你来解决，也不该如此。如果某位团队成员指望你替他们把事修好，你可以这样回应："我理解这很有挑战，但我们一起看看你可以怎么处理它。在寻找解决方案这件事上，我可以怎么支持你？"这种方式把责任交还给他们，赋能他们成长，并对自己的挑战负责。

When you stop trying to solve all problems, you create space for your team to step up, learn, and take responsibility. It also protects your energy and ensures you stay focused on your core responsibilities.

当你不再试图解决所有问题时，就为团队创造了站出来、学习、承担责任的空间。这也保护了你的精力，确保你专注于自己的核心职责。

Remember, being a tech lead isn't about being a superhero. It's about being a guide, a listener, and a supporter, helping your team find their own paths while keeping healthy boundaries.

请记住，做技术负责人不是当超人。而是做一个向导、一个倾听者、一个支持者，帮团队找到他们自己的路，同时保持健康的边界。

Key Takeaway本章要点

One-on-ones are one of your most powerful tools as a tech lead, for managing day-to-day work and for shaping the culture and strength of your team over time. When done well, these conversations become the foundation for trust, growth, and alignment. They help you surface issues early, give people space to be heard, and support their development in ways that are thoughtful and personal.

一对一是你作为技术负责人最强大的工具之一——无论对于日常工作管理，还是对于长期塑造团队文化与实力。做好了，这些对话会成为信任、成长和对齐的基石。它们帮你及早发现问题、给人被倾听的空间，并以体贴、个性化的方式支持他们的发展。

What you bring to the table matters: your presence, your consistency, your ability to truly listen, and your willingness to follow through. You don't need to have all the answers. What matters more is creating a space where people feel safe sharing both their wins and their worries. When team members know they can count on that space, real connection and progress follow.

你带到桌上的东西很重要：你的在场、你的稳定、你真正倾听的能力，以及你跟进到底的意愿。你不需要拥有所有答案。更重要的是创造一个空间，让人们感到可以安全地分享他们的收获，也分享他们的忧虑。当团队成员知道他们可以依靠这个空间时，真正的联结和进步就会随之而来。

If there's one mindset shift to take away, it's this: strong relationships drive strong teams. One-on-ones give you a chance to invest in those relationships consistently and meaningfully.

如果说有一个心态上的转变值得带走，那就是这个：牢固的关系造就强大的团队。一对一则给了你一个机会，去持续而有意义地投资这些关系。

So protect that time. Show up fully. And make it count.

所以，请守护好这段时间。全情投入。让它真正有价值。
